# Univariate Forecasting with `tsgc`

In this section we provide a breakdown of the `tsgc` package in R, which implements a univariate model for time series growth curves-based epidemic forecasting.

The `tsgc` package comes with two example data sets relating to COVID-19: one for Gauteng province in South Africa (i.e. `gauteng` - sourced from South Africa’s official coronavirus online news and information portal) and another for England (i.e. `england` - sourced from the official UK government dashboard for data and insights on coronavirus). In the example that follows, we analyse data on confirmed cases in England, using the following packages.

```{r packages, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Install & load packages
library(tsgc)
library(here)
library(zoo)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(kableExtra)
library(ggplot2)
library(xts)

```

## Forecasting COVID-19 in England

The `england` data set provides a daily time series of new COVID cases reported in England between 20 March 2020 and 22 March 2022. This data includes variables on cumulative new cases, admissions, deaths and hospital cases, specifically for COVID (see below). Please note that the `tsgc` model requires the data series to be in cumulative form and is loaded as an xts object with a date index.

```{r data, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
head(england)
```

We will use the `cum_cases` variable to forecast new COVID cases. **Figure 1** illustrates the 7-day moving average of new cases over this time period (discrete observations, not cumulative).

```{r fig_1, echo=FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 1: New Cases and their centered 7-day moving average for England between 20 March 2020 and 22 March 2022."}
# Get data
Y <- england$cum_cases

# Calculate the 7 day centered moving average
ma.cent <- zoo::rollmean(diff(Y), 7, align = "center") 

# Create df for plot (actual data vs. MA data)
df <- setNames(cbind(diff(Y), ma.cent), c('New Cases', 'Centered 7-day MA'))
df.f <- data.frame(Date = index(df), 
                   New.Cases = coredata(df[,1]),
                   Centered.7.day.MA = coredata(df[,2]))

# Plot Figure 1
ggplot(data = df.f, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = New.Cases, color = "New Cases"), linewidth=0.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Centered.7.day.MA, color = "Centered 7 day MA"), linewidth=1) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
  xlab("Day") +
  ylab("New cases") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "60 days") +
  scale_color_manual(name='', values=c('New Cases'='black', 'Centered 7 day MA'='red')) +
  theme_light(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.2, 0.85)) +
  theme(legend.title=element_text(size=2),legend.text=element_text(size=10)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 10),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

## Model parameters

We begin by specifying a number of options for the forecasting exercise, as defined below.

-   **`Y`** is the data, in the form of time series of cumulative confirmed cases. In this example the object holding this series is called `england`.

-   **`estimation.date.start`** is the date of the first observation in the sample to be used for estimating the model. By default, it is the first date in the `xts` object `Y`. We are interested in the period before the third wave, so our start date is 01 August 2021.

-   **`estimation.date.end`** is the date of the last observation in the sample to be used for estimating the model. By default, it is the last date in the `xts` object `Y`. We are interested in the period before the third wave, so our end date is 20 November 2021.

-   **`n.forecasts`** is the number of days or periods for which forecasts are to be made. E.g., if `n.forecasts = 14`, forecasts will be generated for up to 14 days following `estimation.date.end`.

-   **`q`** is the signal-to-noise ratio, which controls the smoothness of the estimated trend. A lower value will lead to more smoothness. By default, `q = 0.005` is used, which is known to ensure a good balance between the smoothness of the trend and the speed with which changes in estimates respond to new observations (Harvey & Kattuman, 2020). Alongside, `q` can be estimated and compared with the default value.

-   **`confidence.level`** sets the coverage of the confidence intervals for $\ln(g_t)$ which is then used to generate the prediction intervals for forecasts. Here, we use 0.68, corresponding to the probability that the forecast lies within one standard deviation of the point forecast.

-   **`plt.length`** sets a truncation date to enhance the clarity of plots, e.g. showing only the last 30 days of the estimation sample. The date range for plotting can be set as `plt.length` days upto `estimation.date.end`.

-   Optional: **`sea.type`** specifies the type of seasonality and can take `trigonometric` (default) or `none` if there is no seasonal component. 

-   Optional: **`sea.period`** can be used to set the seasonality period by days (default is `7` for weekly patterns), and is not required if `sea.type = 0`

```{r parameters, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Load data
Y <- england$cum_cases

# Set sample period (dates)
estimation.date.start <- as.Date("2021-08-01")
estimation.date.end <- as.Date("2021-11-20")

# Set forecast period (days)
n.forecasts <- 14

# Set smoothness, confidence levels & plot visibility
q <- 0.005
confidence.level <- 0.68
plt.length <- 30

# Seasonality parameters are excluded from this example

```

## Estimating
### Model maths
So what are we going to do with our data, given the parameters above?

The dynamic Gompertz curve model with an integrated random walk (IRW) trend is defined by:

${ \ln g_{t} = \delta_{t} + \varepsilon_{t}, \quad \varepsilon_{t} \sim NID(0, \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2), \quad t = 2, \ldots, T }$

Where:
- $\delta_t = \delta_{t-1} + \gamma_{t-1}$
- $\gamma_t = \gamma_{t-1} + \zeta_t$
  - $\zeta_t \sim NID(0, \sigma_{\zeta}^2)$
  
  Here, the observation disturbances $\varepsilon_t$ and the slope disturbances $\zeta_t$
  are assumed to be independently and identically distributed (iid) normal variables, and
mutually independent.

The signal-to-noise ratio, $q_{\zeta} = \frac{\sigma_{\zeta}^2}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2}$,
controls how quickly the slope $\gamma_t$ responds to new data:
- A **larger ratio** leads to faster changes in the slope.
- A **smaller ratio** results in a smoother slope.

If the model does not include seasonal terms (`sea.type = 'none'`), the priors are:
  
  ${ \begin{pmatrix} \delta_1 \\ \gamma_1 \end{pmatrix} \sim N(a_1, P_1) }$
  
  The **diffuse prior** has $P_1 = \kappa I_{2 \times 2}$, where $\kappa \to \infty$.
This diffuse prior is handled by the `KFAS` package (Helske, 2017).

If the model has a seasonal component (`sea.type = 'trigonometric'`), the vector of prior
means $a_1$ and the prior covariance matrix $P_1$ are extended accordingly.

For more details on the variance matrix $Q$, please refer to the vignette.

The irregular variance is given by $H = \sigma^2_{\varepsilon}$.


### Model fit

Now that we understand what the model will do, we begin by selecting the data series (`Y`) for the defined sample period. Then we estimate the model using a diffuse prior distribution for the initial state vector, using a signal-to-noise ratio of $0.005$ (maintained throughout this example). As mentioned, this value strikes a useful balance between the smoothness of the estimate of the slope parameter $\gamma$, and the speed with which it adapts to new observations.

```{r model_est, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Subset sample period 
y <- Y[estimation.date.start <= index(Y) & index(Y) <= estimation.date.end]

# Fit model with subset & smoothing ratio
model <- SSModelDynamicGompertz$new(Y = y, q = q)
res <- model$estimate()
```

To enable forecast comparisons, create an evaluation sample. This is simply a subset from the actual data of cases **AFTER** the estimation period, converted to the log growth rate.

```{r eval_sample, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# From the original data, subset dates greater than estimation end date and convert to growth rates
y.eval <- Y %>% 
  subset(index(.) > estimation.date.end) %>% # subset
  tsgc::df2ldl() # log growth rate conversion
```

## Results

We can now plot the forecast of the log of the growth rate ($\ln g_t$) of cumulative cases (`Y`). We can compare these forecasts to the actual $\ln g_t$ series by passing the output of our estimation (`res`) along with an evaluation sample (`y.eval`) to a plotting function. 

### Growth rates

We use `plot_forecast` to plot the $\ln(g_t)$ of the 14-day forecast (`res`), relative to the actual data (`y.eval`)

```{r fig_2, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 2: Fourteen-day forecast of growth rate from 21 November 2021, for England."}

# Compare growth rate of projected estimations (res) to actual cases (y.eval)
tsgc::plot_forecast(
  res = res, # projected data (model estimation sample & projection)
  y.eval = y.eval, # actual data (after estimation period)
  n.ahead = n.forecasts,
  plt.start.date = estimation.date.end - plt.length
)
```

### New cases

We use `plot_new_cases` to plot the forecasts of new cases from 21 November 2021, with their prediction intervals.

```{r fig_3, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap = "Figure 3: Fourteen-day forecast of new cases from 21 November 2021 for England"}

# Compare actual data from estimation period to estimated forecast, with confidence level
tsgc::plot_new_cases(
  res = res, # projected data (model estimation sample & projection)
  Y = y, # actual data (from estimation period)
  n.ahead = n.forecasts,
  confidence.level = confidence.level,
  date_format = "%Y-%m-%d",
  plt.start.date = estimation.date.end - plt.length
)
```

### Accuracy

To assess accuracy, we use the `plot_holdout` function to plot forecasts against the actual new cases, that have been held back from the estimation sample. The estimated forecasts are compared to the actual data within the forecast window (`Y.eval`) using mean absolute percentage error (MAPE).

Figure 4 shows that the forecasts were accurate over the 14-days, with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 9%. 


```{r fig_4, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap = "Figure 4: Accuracy of the fourteen-day forecast of new cases from 21 November 2021 for England."}

# Compare estimated forecast (res) to actual data within the forecast window (Y.eval)
tsgc::plot_holdout(res = res, 
                   Y = y,
                   Y.eval = Y[(estimation.date.end+0:n.forecasts)],
                   confidence.level = 0.68,
                   date_format = "%Y-%m-%d")
```

### Reproduction number

The reproduction number ($R_t$) is the average number of people infected by a single person. These numbers and their 68% credible intervals are especially useful for epidemics and can be calculated with this model using generation intervals (i.e.the typical number of days between an infected person becoming infected and them transmitting the disease to someone else). 

Figure 5 reveals that $R_t$ remains above one through the period, indicating that the (third) wave in England has launched by this time.

```{r fig_5, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap = "Figure 5: Reproduction numbers for the 7-day period leading up to 20 November 2021, for England."}
# Set generation interval
gen_int <- 4

# Compute R_t and upper/lower bounds of credible intervals as tibble object
r.t <- fortify(tail(exp(res$get_gy_ci()*gen_int),7)) %>% as_tibble()
names(r.t)<-c("Date", "Rt", "lower", "upper")
r.t$Date <- as.Date(r.t$Date)

# Plot
ggplot(r.t, aes(x = Date)) +
  ylim(0, 1.4)+
  geom_line(aes(y = Rt, color = "Rt")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Rt), color = "red", size = 3) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Date, yend = lower, y = Rt), color = "blue") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Date, yend = upper, y = Rt), color = "blue") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = "68%  Interval"), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype="solid",
             linewidth=1.5, color = "black") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 day") +
  theme_light(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.85, 0.2)) +
  theme(legend.title=element_text(size=2),
        legend.text=element_text(size=10)) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 10),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

**EXPORT RESULTS:** A CSV file (named \verb|y-forecast|) is written to the directory specified. The forecast options specified earlier are retained.

```{r write_results, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval=FALSE}
# Create a directory to store model results
dir.create('results')
res.dir <- paste0(wd, '/results')

# Export results
tsgc::write_results(
 res.dir = res.dir,
 res = res,
 Y = Y,
 n.ahead = n.forecasts,
 confidence.level =  confidence.level
)
```

## Re-initialization

In all countries the coronavirus pandemic was characterized by a series of recurring waves due to a combination of biological, behavioral, and environmental reasons.  In an epidemic, the onset of a new wave is signaled when the slope parameter \(\gamma\), which measures of the growth rate of the growth rate of new cases, rises above zero for a sustained period. Such a super-exponential phase of the epidemic in which the growth rate of new cases is itself increasing over time is typically short.

This section illustrates the reinitialization procedure which allows us to apply the model to the new wave as it begins, without jettisoning information from the wave that has just ended. We extend the estimation window to 31 December 2021, by which date the third wave is well on course with its peak within sight (see Figure 1). All other options remain the same.

```{r change-est-date-end, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Update estimation date end
estimation.date.end <- as.Date("2021-12-31")

# Re-estimate model
y <- Y[estimation.date.start <= index(Y) & index(Y) <= estimation.date.end]
model <- SSModelDynamicGompertz$new(Y = y, q = q)
res <- model$estimate()
```

### Triggering reinitialization

It is not obvious, a priori, when precisely to reinitialize the model. Based on experiments a reasonable option is to reinitialize when the estimate of the slope parameter, $\gamma_t$, breaches a threshold of two standard errors above zero, and at that point backdate reinitialization to when the estimate of $\gamma_t$ first turned positive. In applying the above heuristic there is a choice between the filtered slope estimate and the smoothed slope estimate. Experiments suggests that the greater noisiness of the filtered estimate of $\gamma_t$ often triggers reinitialization too early. The smoothed estimate is more reliable.

Figure 6 shows that for the third wave in England, the smoothed slope estimate exceeded twice its standard error on 06 December 2021, having risen above zero on 06 November 2021. Set the re-initilization date accordingly.

```{r reinit_date, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Extract the smoothed slope and its standard deviation
smoothed.slope.full <- xts::xts(res$output$alphahat[, "slope"], order.by = res$index)
smoothed.slope.sd <- xts::xts(res$output$P[2, 2,-1], order.by = res$index)

# Calculate the 1.5 and 2 SDs of the slope
d2 <- cbind(smoothed.slope.full, sqrt(smoothed.slope.sd),
            1.5 * sqrt(smoothed.slope.sd),
            2 * sqrt(smoothed.slope.sd))
d2.df <- data.frame(date=index(d2), coredata(d2))
colnames(d2.df) <- c("Date", "smoothed.slope", "sd.smoothed.slope",
                     "sd.smoothed.slope.1.5", "sd.smoothed.slope.2")

# Date restriction for visual purposes (Figure 6)
d2.df <- d2.df[d2.df$Date >= as.Date("2021-08-27"), ]

# Identify the trigger date, which is when smoothed slope > 2 (2021-12-06)
trigger.df <- d2.df %>%
  mutate(prev_smoothed.slope = lag(smoothed.slope)) %>%
  filter(smoothed.slope > sd.smoothed.slope.2 & prev_smoothed.slope < sd.smoothed.slope.2)
trigger.df$Date

# Select re-initialization date based on trigger (2021-11-06)
reinit_zero.df <- d2.df %>%
  mutate(prev_smoothed.slope = lag(smoothed.slope)) %>%
  filter(Date < min(trigger.df$Date) & (smoothed.slope > 0 & prev_smoothed.slope < 0)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Date)) %>% slice(1)
reinit_zero.df$Date

# Set re-initialization date
reinit.date <- as.Date(reinit_zero.df$Date, format = date.format) 

```

```{r fig_6, echo=FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap = "Figure 6: Trigger for reinitialization: when filtered slope exceeds twice its standard error above zero, reinitialization is triggered to the date when the filtered slope crossed zero."}

# Create plot
ggplot(data = d2.df, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = smoothed.slope, color = "smoothed.slope"), linewidth=.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sd.smoothed.slope, color = "sd.smoothed.slope"), linetype = "solid", linewidth=.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sd.smoothed.slope.1.5, color = "sd.smoothed.slope.1.5"), linetype = "solid", linewidth=.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sd.smoothed.slope.2, color = "sd.smoothed.slope.2"), linetype = "solid", linewidth=.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", color = "black",linewidth = 1)+
  geom_vline(data = trigger.df, aes(xintercept = Date), linetype = "solid", size = .5, color = "black")+
  geom_vline(data = reinit_zero.df, aes(xintercept = Date), linetype = "solid",size = 1, color = "black")+
  xlab("Day") +
  ylab("Slope") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "10 days") +
  scale_color_manual(name='',values=c('smoothed.slope'='red', 
                                      'sd.smoothed.slope'='blue', 
                                      'sd.smoothed.slope.1.5'='green', 
                                      'sd.smoothed.slope.2'='black'))+
  theme_light(base_size = 11)+
  theme(legend.title=element_text(size=2),legend.text=element_text(size=6))+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))



```

### Estimating the reinitialized model

`SSModelDynGompertzReinit` takes the same arguments as `SSModelDynGompertz`, with the addition of the `reinit.dates` argument.

```{r reinit_model, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}

# Estimate re-initialized model
model <- SSModelDynGompertzReinit$new(Y = y, q = q, reinit.date = reinit.date)
res.reinit <- model$estimate()

# Reinitialize the original dataframe
Y.reinit <- Y %>%
  reinitialise_dataframe(., reinit.date)

# Re-initialized the evaluation sample
y.eval.reinit <- Y %>%
  reinitialise_dataframe(., reinit.date) %>% # Select data after reinit date (important for growth calculation)
  df2ldl()  %>% # Log growth transformation
  subset(index(.) > estimation.date.end) # Subset to after estimation end date

```

### Re-initialized results
```{r fig_7, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Compare growth rate of projected estimations (res) to actual cases (y.eval)
tsgc::plot_forecast(
    res=res.reinit,
    y.eval = y.eval.reinit,
    n.ahead = n.forecasts,
    plt.start.date = estimation.date.end - plt.length
    )
```

```{r fig_8, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Compare actual data from estimation period to estimated forecast, with confidence level
tsgc::plot_new_cases(
  res=res.reinit, 
  Y=Y.reinit, 
  n.ahead=n.forecasts,
  confidence.level=confidence.level,
  date_format="%Y-%m-%d",
  plt.start.date = estimation.date.end - plt.length
  )
```


```{r fig_9, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Compare estimated forecast (res) to actual data within the forecast window (Y.eval)
tsgc::plot_holdout(res = res.reinit, 
                   Y=Y.reinit[index(y)],
                   Y.eval = Y[(estimation.date.end+0:n.forecasts)],
                   confidence.level = 0.68,
                   date_format = "%Y-%m-%d")
```
